citations.quote: Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval and let $a\le t_1<\cdots<t_r\le b$ with $r\ge2$. A natural cubic spline with knots $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ is a $C^2$ function on $[a,b]$ that is a polynomial of degree at most three on every $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, has second derivative zero at $t_1$ and $t_r$, and is extended linearly on $[a,t_1]$ and $[t_r,b]$ when those intervals are nonempty. The knots $t_j$ are the distinct breakpoints; repeated observations at the same input do not create additional knots.

derivations.claim: Put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i$ and $d_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/h_i$. For $r=2$ there are no interior second derivatives to solve. For $r\ge3$, let $A$ be the $(r-2)\times(r-2)$ symmetric tridiagonal matrix with diagonal entry $2(h_{i-1}+h_i)$ in row $i$ and adjacent off-diagonal entries $h_i$. For a nonzero vector $v=(v_2,\ldots,v_{r-1})$, using $2v_iv_{i+1}\ge-v_i^2-v_{i+1}^2$ gives $v^TAv\ge\sum_{i=2}^{r-1}(h_{i-1}+h_i)v_i^2>0.$ Thus $A$ is positive definite and invertible, so the displayed system has exactly one solution $M_2,\ldots,M_{r-1}$.

On $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$, define $s_i(x)=\frac{M_i(x_{i+1}-x)^3+M_{i+1}(x-x_i)^3}{6h_i}+\left(y_i-\frac{M_i h_i^2}{6}\right)\frac{x_{i+1}-x}{h_i}+\left(y_{i+1}-\frac{M_{i+1}h_i^2}{6}\right)\frac{x-x_i}{h_i}.$ Direct substitution gives $s_i(x_i)=y_i$, $s_i(x_{i+1})=y_{i+1}$, and $s_i''(x_i)=M_i$, $s_i''(x_{i+1})=M_{i+1}$. Its endpoint slopes are $d_i+M_i h_i/6+M_{i+1}h_i/3$ and $d_i-M_i h_i/3-M_{i+1}h_i/6$. The tridiagonal equation at $x_i$ says the right slope from $s_{i-1}$ equals the left slope from $s_i$. Hence the pieces join $C^1$; their second derivatives are linear with the same nodal values, so they join $C^2$. At the extreme knots $M_1=M_r=0$, so adjoining the tangent line gives the required linear tails and preserves $C^2$. For $r=2$, the formula is the straight line between the two values and the same endpoint argument applies.

Any natural cubic interpolant has nodal second derivatives with $M_1=M_r=0$. Equality of its adjacent endpoint slopes forces the displayed tridiagonal equations, so by step 1.1 its nodal second derivatives equal the constructed ones. On each interval, the difference from $s_i$ is a cubic with zero second derivative at both endpoints; its second derivative is affine and therefore zero throughout, so the difference is affine and vanishes at both endpoint values. It is identically zero. Thus the interpolant is unique.

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $n\ge p+1$, and $a<b$. A clamped knot vector is a nondecreasing finite sequence
$$\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_{p+1}=a<\xi_{p+2}\le\cdots\le\xi_n<\xi_{n+1}=\cdots=\xi_{n+p+1}=b,$$
with $\xi_j<\xi_{j+p+1}$ for every $1\le j\le n$. Empty interior ranges are omitted. The multiplicity $\mu(\eta)$ of an interior knot $\eta$ is its number of occurrences among $\xi_{p+2},\ldots,\xi_n$.

Write $\mathcal P_p$ for the real polynomials of degree at most $p$. The degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ consists of functions that restrict to a member of $\mathcal P_p$ on each nonempty knot interval and whose derivatives through order $p-\mu(\eta)$ agree across each interior knot $\eta$. The convention $C^{-1}$ means that no matching condition is imposed. For this piecewise definition, take knot cells left-closed and right-open; at a knot with no matching condition, the value is the one from the cell on its right, and at $b$ use the left limit. Thus the function value at a discontinuous knot is specified.

The degree-zero B-spline is $B_{j,0,\xi}=\mathbf 1_{[\xi_j,\xi_{j+1})}$. For $p\ge1$, define recursively
$$B_{j,p,\xi}(x)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}B_{j,p-1,\xi}(x)+\frac{\xi_{j+p+1}-x}{\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1}}B_{j+1,p-1,\xi}(x),$$
where a term with zero denominator is defined to be zero. At $b$, set $B_{j,p,\xi}(b)$ equal to its left limit. The basis and regularity properties of this recursively defined family are proved in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]].

derivations.claim: For $p=0$, support, piecewise degree, and nonnegativity follow from the indicator definition in [F1]. Inductively, each degree-$p$ term is a lower-degree spline multiplied by an affine factor; on the lower-degree spline's support that factor is nonnegative, and the two supports lie inside $[\xi_j, \xi_{j+p+1}]$. Thus support, degree at most $p$, and nonnegativity hold for every $p$.

Define $\psi_{j,0}(y)=1$ and $\psi_{j,p}(y)=\prod_{r=1}^{p}(y-\xi_{j+r})$. Factoring $\psi_{j,p-1}$ gives $(y-x)\psi_{j,p-1}(y)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}\psi_{j,p}(y)+\frac{\xi_{j+p}-x}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}\psi_{j-1,p}(y),$ with zero-denominator terms omitted. For $p=0$, $(y-x)^p=1$ is the local identity on any nonempty knot interval. If the identity holds for degree $p-1$, multiply it by $y-x$, apply the displayed dual-polynomial identity to each summand, and regroup the two contributions to each coefficient using the recurrence in [F1]. The endpoint terms vanish by local support. Hence, for $x\in[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, $(y-x)^p=\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}\psi_{i,p}(y)B_{i,p,\xi}(x).$

Let the distinct interior knots be $\eta_1<\cdots<\eta_s$ with multiplicities $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_s$. For $k\ge1$ set $u_{r,k}(x)=(x-\eta_r)^k\mathbf1_{[\eta_r,\infty)}(x)$ and set $u_{r,0}(x)=\mathbf1_{[\eta_r,\infty)}(x)$; the value at $\eta_r$ follows the right-cell convention of [F1]. The functions $1,x,\ldots,x^p$ together with $u_{r,k}$ for $p-\mu_r+1\le k\le p$ span $S_{p,\xi}$: start with the polynomial on the first interval, then at each knot the difference of adjacent pieces has its derivatives through $p-\mu_r$ equal to zero, so it is a linear combination of the listed powers, including the right-continuous step when $\mu_r=p+1$. They are independent because restriction to successive knot intervals first forces the initial polynomial coefficients, then each new knot's coefficients, to vanish. Thus $\dim S_{p,\xi}=p+1+\sum_r\mu_r=n$.

Differentiate the identity in step 1.2 exactly $p-k$ times in $y$ and set $y=0$, for each $0\le k\le p$. Since $\frac{d^{p-k}}{dy^{p-k}}(y-x)^p|_{y=0}=\frac{p!}{k!}(-x)^k$, this yields $x^k=\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}\left[(-1)^k\frac{k!}{p!}\psi_{i, p}^{(p-k)}(0)\right]B_{i,p,\xi}(x).$ The coefficients do not depend on $m$, so this is a single expansion valid on every knot interval. Linear combination proves reproduction of every member of $\mathcal P_p$.

For $p=1$, differentiating the two affine pieces gives the derivative formula below. For $p\ge2$, differentiate the recurrence in [F1] and substitute the degree-$(p-1)$ formula inductively. The coefficients of $B_{j,p-2,\xi}$ and $B_{j+2,p-2,\xi}$ become respectively $p(x-\xi_j)/((\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)(\xi_{j+p-1}-\xi_j))$ and $-p(\xi_{j+p+1}-x)/((\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+2}))$; the middle coefficient is the sum $\frac{\xi_{j+p}-x-(p-1)(x-\xi_j)}{(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})}+\frac{-(x-\xi_{j+1})+(p-1)(\xi_{j+p+1}-x)}{(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})},$ The target middle coefficient from expanding the right side of the claimed formula with [F1] is $\frac{p(\xi_{j+p}-x)}{(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})}-\frac{p(x-\xi_{j+1})}{(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})}.$ The first summand in the previous display differs from the first target summand by $-(p-1)/(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})$, while the second differs from the second target summand by $+(p-1)/(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})$; these excess terms cancel. Zero-denominator terms vanish by [F1]. Thus, on each open knot interval, $B'_{j,p,\xi}=p\left(\frac{B_{j,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}-\frac{B_{j+1,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1}}\right).$

Taking $k=0$ in step 2.1 gives $\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}B_{i,p,\xi}(x)=1$. Step 2.1 also shows that these $p+1$ active functions span $\mathcal P_p$ on the interval. Because $\dim\mathcal P_p=p+1$, they are linearly independent there and are a local basis.

Induct on $p$. If the knot multiplicity $\mu\le p-1$, the lower-degree splines in the recurrence are continuous there by induction, so the recurrence makes $B_{j,p,\xi}$ continuous; the derivative formula then makes its derivative $C^{p-1-\mu}$, hence $B_{j,p,\xi}\in C^{p-\mu}$. If $\mu=p$, a B-spline whose support crosses the repeated knot has one nonzero piece on either side, namely $(x-\xi_j)^p/(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)^p$ and $(\xi_{j+p+1}-x)^p/(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})^p$; both one-sided limits equal $1$, while any B-spline not crossing it has zero endpoint value there. If $\mu=p+1$, the required order is $C^{-1}$ and no matching is asserted.

The smoothness and piecewise-degree properties from steps 1.1 and 3.2 put every B-spline in $S_{p,\xi}$. If a linear combination of all $n$ B-splines is zero, then on every nonempty knot interval its active coefficients vanish by the local basis property in step 3.1. Each B-spline has a nonempty support interval by the clamped-knot hypothesis, so every coefficient occurs on at least one such interval and is zero. The B-splines are therefore $n$ independent members of the $n$-dimensional space in step 1.3, hence form its basis. The unique global expansion includes every polynomial from step 2.1.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Let $r\ge2$, $a\le x_1<\cdots<x_r\le b$, and $y_1,\ldots,y_r\in\mathbb R$. There is exactly one natural cubic spline $s$ on $[a,b]$ with $s(x_i)=y_i$ for each $i$. On each interval $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ it is the cubic with endpoint values $y_i,y_{i+1}$ and endpoint second derivatives $M_i,M_{i+1}$, where $M_1=M_r=0$ and the interior values solve the positive-definite tridiagonal system
$$h_{i-1}M_{i-1}+2(h_{i-1}+h_i)M_i+h_iM_{i+1}=6\left(\frac{y_{i+1}-y_i}{h_i}-\frac{y_i-y_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}\right),\quad 2\le i\le r-1,$$
with $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$. The interpolant is linear outside $[x_1,x_r]$.

Assume AC. Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval, let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n\in([a,b]\times\mathbb R)^n$, assume at least two distinct input values, and let $\lambda>0$. For $g\in W^{2,2}(a,b)$ use its unique continuous representative on $[a,b]$ supplied by the one-dimensional Sobolev representative theorem. The natural cubic smoothing spline is the unique minimizer, whose existence and uniqueness are proved in [[thm-natural-cubic-smoothing-spline-exists-uniquely]], of
$$J(g)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-g(x_i))^2+\lambda\int_a^b|D^2g(t)|^2\,dt.$$

The requirement of two distinct inputs is essential. The penalty is the squared $L^2$ norm of the second weak derivative; the data term uses the distinct-input interpolation convention in [[def-natural-cubic-spline]].

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

derivations.claim: Let $g\in W^{2,2}(a,b)$ and use the continuous representative in [F2] for $g$ and $g'$. The Countable Choice convention in [F1] and the choice hypotheses for [F2] are available by [F5] and [A1]. Interpolate the values $g(t_j)$ by the natural cubic $s$ from [F3], and put $h=g-s$. Then $h(t_j)=0$ for every $j$. On each interval between distinct knots, $s'''$ is constant; on the two linear tails, $s''=s'''=0$.

The natural spline with knots $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ is uniquely determined by its nodal vector $z=(s(t_1),\ldots,s(t_r))\in\mathbb R^r$ by [F3]. The tridiagonal system in the interpolation proof is linear in its data, and the interval formula is linear in the nodal values and second derivatives; hence $z\mapsto s_z''$ is linear into the finite-dimensional space of piecewise-linear functions. Therefore $R(z)=\int|s_z''|^2$ is a finite nonnegative quadratic form. In these coordinates $J(s)=\sum_j\sum_{i:x_i=t_j}(y_i-z_j)^2+\lambda R(z)$. The data term has positive-definite diagonal quadratic part because every $t_j$ occurs at least once. Adding the nonnegative quadratic form $\lambda R$ leaves a positive-definite quadratic objective, which has a unique minimizer by completing the square.

On each knot interval, the product $s''h'$ is absolutely continuous, so the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $\int s''h''=[s''h']-\int s'''h'$. Summing over the intervals, the interior boundary terms cancel because $s''$ and $h'$ are continuous. At each outer endpoint, $s''=0$ either on a linear tail or by the natural condition when that endpoint is a knot. The remaining terms are $-s'''|_{(t_j,t_{j+1})}(h(t_{j+1})-h(t_j))=0$. Thus $\int_a^b s''h''=0$.

Since $g=s+h$, expanding the square and applying step 2.1 yields $\int_a^b|g''|^2=\int_a^b|s''|^2+\int_a^b|h''|^2.$ Also $s(x_i)=g(x_i)$ for every observed input, so their data residual terms agree. Therefore $J(g)=J(s)+\lambda\int_a^b|h''|^2\ge J(s)$, with equality only if $h''=0$ almost everywhere.

Let $s_*$ be this finite-dimensional minimizer. Step 3.1 shows $J(g)\ge J(s_*)$ for every $g\in W^{2,2}$. If equality holds, then $h''=0$ almost everywhere, so by [F2] $h$ is affine; its zero values at the two distinct knots $t_1,t_r$ force $h=0$. Thus $s_*$ is the unique minimizer over the full Sobolev class, and its natural cubic form and linear tails are those of [F3].

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. For every $v\in V$, the vector $P_Wv$ is the unique point of $W$ nearest to $v$: for every $w\in W$,

$$\lVert v-P_Wv\rVert\le\lVert v-w\rVert,$$

with equality if and only if $w=P_Wv$.

Let $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ be an orthonormal basis of a subspace $W$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. Then

$$P_Wv=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i.$$

The map $P_W$ is linear, with image $W$, kernel $W^\perp$, and $P_W^2=P_W$. Moreover, regarding both projections as endomorphisms of $V$,

$$I-P_W=P_{W^\perp}.$$

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

derivations.claim: On any neighborhood $J=[c,d]$, use the continuous representatives of $D^jf$, $0\le j\le l$, supplied by [F2]. Their Sobolev-class convention [F1] and the choice hypotheses for [F2] are available under [A1] by [F5]. Repeated integration by parts for absolutely continuous functions gives the Taylor identity $f(x)-T_{c,l}f(x)=\frac1{l!}\int_c^x(x-t)^lD^{l+1}f(t)\,dt,$ where $T_{c,l}f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^lD^jf(c)(x-c)^j/j!$. For completeness, the case $l=0$ is the increment formula in [F2]; passing from order $l-1$ to $l$ integrates $\int_c^x(x-t)^{l-1}D^lf(t)dt$ by parts with antiderivative $-(x-t)^l/l$, producing the degree-$l$ endpoint term and the displayed remainder. Hölder [F3] therefore gives $\|f-T_{c,l}f\|_{L^q(J)}\le |J|^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q(J)}/l!$, including $q=\infty$.

Choose $c$ as the left endpoint of $J_m$ and write $T=T_{c,l}f$. Since $Q$ reproduces $\mathcal P_l$, $QT=T$. The triangle inequality and the local stability in the definition give $\|f-Qf\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le\|f-T\|_{L^q(I_m)}+\|Q(f-T)\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le(1+C_Q)\|f-T\|_{L^q(J_m)}.$ Apply step 1.1 and $|J_m|\le Mh_m$ to get the stated local estimate.

Raise the local estimates to the $q$th power and sum over the disjoint mesh cells. Each point belongs to at most $M$ neighborhoods, so $\sum_m\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q(J_m)}^q\le M\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q([a,b])}^q$. Taking the $q$th root and using $h_m\le h$ gives the stated global bound for finite $q$. For $q=\infty$, take the maximum of the local bounds; the factor $M^{1/q}$ is $1$.

For a uniform mesh with interior knots repeated $p+1$ times, $S_{p,\xi}$ is the space of independent degree-$p$ polynomials on the cells by the definition and basis theorem. Define $Q_hf$ on each cell as the orthogonal projection of $f$ onto $\mathcal P_p$. By [F4] it is linear and contractive in $L^2$; it depends only on that cell, takes values in $S_{p,\xi}$, and fixes every member of $\mathcal P_p$. Thus it satisfies the local quasi-interpolant hypotheses with one-cell neighborhoods, $M=1$, and $C_Q=1$. Applying steps 1.1, 2.1, and 3.1 with $l=s-1$ gives $\|f-Q_hf\|_{L^2}\le 2h^s\|D^sf\|_{L^2}/(s-1)!$ for $1\le s\le p+1$.

Let $p_K(x)=(B_{1,p,\xi}(x),\ldots,B_{K,p,\xi}(x))^T$ be a specified degree-$p$ B-spline basis on the data domain, and let $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be observed real-valued data. Form the design matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times K}$ with row $p_K(X_i)^T$. The **series least-squares fitted training vector** is
$$\widehat{\mathbf g}_K=\Pi_{\operatorname{col}(P)}\mathbf Y,$$
the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^T$ onto the column space of $P$. Conditional on the realized design, this is the fixed-design least-squares fitted vector of [[def-fixed-design-projection-estimator]]. Equivalently, it is $P\widehat\beta$ for any minimizer $\widehat\beta$ of $\|\mathbf Y-P\beta\|_2^2$; all such minimizers have the same fitted training vector. The training prediction loss relative to a specified target vector $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$ is $n^{-1}\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2$. This definition specifies training fitted values and makes no test-risk assertion.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. For every $v\in V$, the vector $P_Wv$ is the unique point of $W$ nearest to $v$: for every $w\in W$,

$$\lVert v-P_Wv\rVert\le\lVert v-w\rVert,$$

with equality if and only if $w=P_Wv$.

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

Let $n,d\in\mathbb N$ with $n,d\ge1$, and let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ be a fixed design
matrix, and write $V_X:=\{X\theta:\theta\in\mathbb R^d\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$
for its column space. For an observed vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, the **fixed-design
least-squares fitted vector** is

$$\widehat\mu_X(y):=P_{V_X}y,$$

where $P_{V_X}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $V_X$, as defined in
[[def-orthogonal-projection]]. It is uniquely defined even when $X$ is rank
deficient. The nearest-point characterization in
[[thm-orthogonal-projection-is-the-unique-nearest-point]] says that
$\widehat\mu_X(y)$ minimizes $\|y-v\|_2$ over $v\in V_X$. This item defines the
fitted vector; it does not select a coefficient representation $\widehat\theta$.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Write $\mathbf X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ and $\epsilon_i=Y_i-g_0(X_i)$. For fixed $\mathbf x$, set $\kappa_1=\kappa(x_1,\cdot)$ and, for $1\le m<n$, apply [F10] to $\kappa_m$ and $\kappa(x_{m+1},\cdot)$ to obtain $\kappa_{m+1}$; both factors are probability measures, so the rectangle formula gives total mass one at each stage. Induction gives the finite product probability measure $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\cdot)$ with rectangle values $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\prod_iB_i)=\prod_i\kappa(x_i,B_i)$. The response rectangles form a pi-system because intersections of rectangles are rectangles, and [F5] says they generate the response product sigma-algebra. On response rectangles the evaluation is Borel in $\mathbf x$ by [F4] and [F10]. Because $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, the class of sets with Borel evaluation contains the whole space, is closed under complements by subtraction from $1$, and is closed under disjoint countable unions by limits of partial sums; [F11] therefore gives measurability for every response Borel set. For rectangles $A=\prod_iA_i$ and $B=\prod_iB_i$, iid sampling gives $P(\mathbf X\in A,\mathbf Y\in B)=\prod_i\int_{A_i}\kappa(x,B_i)P_X(dx)$, and repeated Tonelli [F13] gives $\int_A\kappa_n(\mathbf x,B)P_X^{\otimes n}(d\mathbf x)=\prod_i\int_{A_i}\kappa(x,B_i)P_X(dx).$ For fixed response Borel $B$, the left side of the target identity is a finite measure in $A$; the right side is also a measure by [F12], applied to the nonnegative measurable function $\mathbf x\mapsto\kappa_n(\mathbf x,B)$. Design rectangles form a pi-system because intersections are rectangles and generate the design product sigma-algebra by [F5], so [F11] extends the equality to every design Borel $A$. For each such $A$, both sides are finite measures in $B$: countable additivity on the right follows from countable additivity of $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\cdot)$ and monotone convergence, and their common total mass is $P_X^{\otimes n}(A)$ because the joint design marginal is $P_X^{\otimes n}$ and $\kappa_n$ is a probability kernel. Thus the response sets $B$ for which the identity holds for every $A$ form a Dynkin system (complements use the common total mass); they contain the response rectangles, so [F11] gives equality for every response Borel set. Hence $\kappa_n$ is a conditional law of $\mathbf Y$ given $\mathbf X$. Under this product law the residuals are conditionally independent, have conditional means zero by [A2], and conditional second moments at most $\Delta$. Hence $E[\epsilon_i\epsilon_j\mid\mathbf X]=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $E[\epsilon_i^2\mid\mathbf X]\le\Delta$.

Let $Q=\Pi_{\operatorname{col}(D)}$. The matrix $Q$ is a Borel function of $D$: partition the finite-dimensional matrix space by rank and, within each positive-rank stratum, by the lexicographically first nonzero maximal minor; on each resulting Borel piece, the corresponding independent columns form a matrix $C$. The Gram matrix $C^TC$ is positive definite, and $C(C^TC)^{-1}C^T$ is symmetric, idempotent, and has image $\operatorname{col}(C)=\operatorname{col}(D)$, so it is the orthogonal projection; at rank zero put $Q=0$. These finitely many Borel formulas show that $Q$ is measurable with respect to $\mathbf X$. Its rank $r$ is at most $K$. Scanning the finitely many columns and retaining a column precisely when it is not in the span of those already retained gives a basis of $\operatorname{col}(D)$; applying Gram–Schmidt [F7] gives an $n\times r$ matrix $U$ with orthonormal columns spanning that subspace. For any $v$, $UU^Tv$ belongs to $\operatorname{col}(D)$ and $U^T(v-UU^Tv)=0$, so its residual is orthogonal to the columns of $U$ and hence to $\operatorname{col}(D)$. By the uniqueness in [F9], $Q=UU^T$; therefore $\operatorname{tr}(Q)=\operatorname{tr}(U^TU)=r\le K$. Since $Q_{ii}=\|Qe_i\|_2^2\ge0$, step 1.1 gives $E[\epsilon^TQ\epsilon\mid\mathbf X]=\sum_iQ_{ii}E[\epsilon_i^2\mid\mathbf X]\le\Delta\operatorname{tr}(Q)\le\Delta K.$

Write $\mathbf g=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$. From [F1] and [F8], $\widehat{\mathbf g}_K=Q\mathbf Y$, and $\mathbf Y=\mathbf g+\epsilon$. In the orthogonal decomposition $\mathbb R^n=\operatorname{col}(D)\oplus\operatorname{col}(D)^\perp$, the projection [F9] is identity on the first summand and zero on the second, so $Q^T=Q=Q^2$, $\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g\|_2^2=\|Q\epsilon-(I-Q)\mathbf g\|_2^2=\epsilon^TQ\epsilon+\|(I-Q)\mathbf g\|_2^2,$ because $Q(I-Q)=0$. For $\bar{\mathbf g}=D\bar\beta_K\in\operatorname{col}(D)$, $(I-Q)\bar{\mathbf g}=0$; the nearest-point property [F6] therefore gives $\|(I-Q)\mathbf g\|_2^2\le\|\mathbf g-\bar{\mathbf g}\|_2^2$.

Taking expectations in step 3.1, applying step 2.1 and then iid sampling with [A3] yields $E\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g\|_2^2\le\Delta K+E\sum_{i=1}^n\{g_0(X_i)-p_K(X_i)^T\bar\beta_K\}^2\le\Delta K+nC^2K^{-2\gamma}.$ Divide by $n$ to obtain the claimed expected empirical training-risk bound.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $n,K\ge1$, let $X_i\in[a,b]$ and $Y_i\in\mathbb R$ be iid pairs, and suppose the one-observation law is $P_X(dx)\kappa(x,dy)$ for a supplied Borel probability kernel $\kappa$ from $([a,b],\mathcal B([a,b]))$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Assume a Borel function $g_0:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is supplied such that, for $P_X$-almost every $x$, $\int |y|\,\kappa(x,dy)<\infty$, $g_0(x)=\int y\,\kappa(x,dy)$, and $\int (y-g_0(x))^2\,\kappa(x,dy)\le\Delta$ for a finite $\Delta\ge0$. Let $p_K:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^K$ be a fixed Borel $K$-dimensional spline basis and assume a deterministic $\bar\beta_K\in\mathbb R^K$ and constants $C,\gamma>0$ satisfy
$$E\{g_0(X)-p_K(X)^T\bar\beta_K\}^2\le C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume a Borel function $g_0:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is supplied such that, for $P_X$-almost every $x$, $\int |y|\,\kappa(x,dy)<\infty$, $g_0(x)=\int y\,\kappa(x,dy)$, and $\int (y-g_0(x))^2\,\kappa(x,dy)\le\Delta$ for a finite $\Delta\ge0$. Let $p_K:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^K$ be a fixed Borel $K$-dimensional spline basis and assume a deterministic $\bar\beta_K\in\mathbb R^K$ and constants $C,\gamma>0$ satisfy
$$E\{g_0(X)-p_K(X)^T\bar\beta_K\}^2\le C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
Then, with the fitted training vector $\widehat{\mathbf g}_K$ from [[def-series-spline-least-squares]] and $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$,
$$E\left[\frac1n\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2\right]\le\frac{\Delta K}{n}+C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
This is expected empirical training-design loss.

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $n\ge p+1$, and $a<b$. A clamped knot vector is a nondecreasing finite sequence
$$\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_{p+1}=a<\xi_{p+2}\le\cdots\le\xi_n<\xi_{n+1}=\cdots=\xi_{n+p+1}=b,$$
with $\xi_j<\xi_{j+p+1}$ for every $1\le j\le n$. Empty interior ranges are omitted. The multiplicity $\mu(\eta)$ of an interior knot $\eta$ is its number of occurrences among $\xi_{p+2},\ldots,\xi_n$.

Write $\mathcal P_p$ for the real polynomials of degree at most $p$. The degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ consists of functions that restrict to a member of $\mathcal P_p$ on each nonempty knot interval and whose derivatives through order $p-\mu(\eta)$ agree across each interior knot $\eta$. The convention $C^{-1}$ means that no matching condition is imposed. For this piecewise definition, take knot cells left-closed and right-open; at a knot with no matching condition, the value is the one from the cell on its right, and at $b$ use the left limit. Thus the function value at a discontinuous knot is specified.

The degree-zero B-spline is $B_{j,0,\xi}=\mathbf 1_{[\xi_j,\xi_{j+1})}$. For $p\ge1$, define recursively
$$B_{j,p,\xi}(x)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}B_{j,p-1,\xi}(x)+\frac{\xi_{j+p+1}-x}{\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1}}B_{j+1,p-1,\xi}(x),$$
where a term with zero denominator is defined to be zero. At $b$, set $B_{j,p,\xi}(b)$ equal to its left limit. The basis and regularity properties of this recursively defined family are proved in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]].

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.
